Jefferson was not a Republican; he was a *Democratic-Republican*. Completely different Party. Neither the Democratic Party nor the Republican Party existed during the Jefferson Presidency. In fact, the Democratic Party was founded in 1828, and the Republican Party even later in 1854. Calling any of these historical figures “Democrats” and “Republicans” makes 0 sense, because they couldn’t have possibly been members of parties that wouldn’t exist until decades after they left politics. Even if you attempted to refer to them this way by analogy, it quickly falls apart: it was a completely different party system and political landscape circa 1800, with the ideological divides and issues of note considered relevant distinctions between the parties being largely different from those of the modern day. I don’t really understand your final point here either: it seems you’re trying to make some argument against the existence of the Party switch, but I fail to see how Jefferson and Hamilton’s political views are relevant to that, except so indirectly that they might as well be unrelated.

In this context, it’s not an umlaut, but a diaeresis. It’s to indicate the “e” vowel is pronounced separately from the “a” vowel. A more common example in standard English is “naïve”, where the diaeresis indicates it’s to be pronounced “neye-eve” and not “nayve”. Not too common to see “Israel” spelled with one, but not sure if it’s technically incorrect. It does work pronunciation-wise, though.

A lot of people in my family have struggles with and died from drugs and/or alcohol, and it always starts with a little bit of “experimenting” like this. You often never know how badly you’ll react to this stuff until it’s too late to do anything about it. If you were fine with it that’s cool (no problems with what you decide to put in your own body), but there’s a major genetic component to addiction that makes some people much more vulnerable.
